title: Regulatory Relief for Certain Stationary Sources To Promote American Mineral Security
summary:
The Administration has issued a proclamation giving certain copper smelters a two‑year extension on meeting new federal pollution rules, saying the technology needed to comply isn’t yet commercially available and that keeping domestic copper capacity online is a national security priority.

The move targets the Environmental Protection Agency’s 2024 rule that tightened emissions limits for primary copper smelters. The proclamation argues the rule would place heavy burdens on a tiny, aging industry—only two primary smelters were operating in 2024—and could force closures that increase reliance on foreign processing. During the two‑year window, affected facilities will follow the standards that were in place before the 2024 rule. The annex lists Freeport‑McMoRan’s Miami Smelter in Arizona as covered.

Who stands to benefit? Domestic copper producers gain breathing room to plan upgrades, avoid shutdowns, and keep workers on the job. Companies across energy, defense, and manufacturing that depend on a stable copper supply may also benefit from reduced supply risk and price volatility. Supporters see this as a practical step to protect a critical material while industry catches up.

Who could be negatively affected? Communities near smelters and public health advocates may see this as a setback, since stricter limits are delayed and hazardous emissions could remain higher for longer. States and local governments focused on cleaner air might face tougher trade‑offs, and firms that already invested to meet the new standards could view the delay as uneven treatment.

What to watch next: whether industry uses the extra time to advance workable pollution controls, how air quality trends in nearby communities, and if legal or policy challenges emerge. The debate will likely center on balancing reliable mineral supply with timely health and environmental protections.
